newsitem.title: GERMANY: FORECAST - German 96, 97 growth seen restrained.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST - German 96, 97 growth seen restrained.

text.p: The German economy will register somewhat restrained levels of GDP growth in 1996, analysts say, with forecasts for average growth rates confined to around 1.2 percent.
A Reuters survey published on Wednesday polled a total of 34 analysts on their outlook for GDP growth on a quarterly basis and for 1996 and 1997.
The figure for 1997 is more optimistic, with the average forecast for around 2.2 percent growth in GDP in that year, with the lowest forecast at 1.5 percent coming from four respondents.

"Next year the world will see slow growth without major swings from quarter to quarter in one or the other direction. This will be a moderate growth, initially led by exports and then by domestic factors," said Mathias Haffner, economist at BZW in Frankfurt.
There are statistical problems with the current year, as the second quarter could plausibly be revised downwards, which is built into their calculations, said Haffner.
BZW's forecast for 1996 is for GDP growth of 1.2 percent and for 2.5 percent in 1997.
As far as the current account goes, Haffner said: "We are quite negative on the current account. We are not expecting any special improvements.
"One of the main factors in this has been the decline in Germany's foreign interest payments in recent years, a long-term factor."
"Germany is still a net creditor and is owed more by other countries than it owes them, but since German reunification that situation is turning around," said Haffner.

The top-end forecast for Germany's current account in full-year 1996 in the Reuters survey, from 27 respondents, was for a deficit of 14 billion marks from Yamaichi, while the lowest forecast, from JP Morgan was for a deficit of 35.7 billion marks.

Looking at Germany's visible trade, the top-end forecast for 1996 came from IBJ Deutschland, for a surplus of 110 billion marks while the London Business School came in at the lower end with 76.4 billion marks.
"We see export as a motor for growth, but it's a little difficult to make forecasts because the previous year's information isn't complete," said Haffner.
